The Grey sunbird Cyanomitra veroxii, a nectarivorous species endemic to coastal and montane forests of southern and eastern Africa, displays life-history traits that reflect its energetic reliance on floral resources. At the elevated body temperatures typical of active thermoregulation in this species (40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]), the maximum basal metabolic rate has been measured at 24 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 24 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a value consistent with the moderate metabolic demands of a small-bodied passerine. During incubation, eggs maintained at a lower thermal regime of 34 °C [T = 34 °C] hatch after an incubation period of approximately 14 days [ab = approximately 14 days], a duration extrapolated from observations on the closely related Golden-winged Sunbird Drepanorhynchus reichenowi. This relatively brief incubation period aligns with the general pattern among Nectariniidae, where rapid embryonic development is typical despite the altricial condition of the hatchlings. Field data on birth masses remain scarce, but available records indicate that newly hatched individuals emerge at an initial wet weight of 1.44 grams [Ww0 = 1.44 grams], a modest size that necessitates intensive parental provisioning during the nestling phase. This energetic investment is further underscored by the nestling growth trajectory and the timing of subsequent developmental milestones under optimal thermal conditions.

Reproductive output in Cyanomitra veroxii follows a pattern typical of many tropical sunbirds, where clutch size is relatively small and breeding events are spaced across the favourable season. Females typically produce a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year], with each clutch containing between 1 and 3 eggs [N_R_i = each clutch containing between 1 and 3 eggs]. Given that only one clutch is attempted annually, with each clutch containing between 1 and 3 eggs [N_R_i = each clutch containing between 1 and 3 eggs], this strategy prioritizes high parental investment per nestling over multiple breeding attempts and reflects the energetic constraints imposed by a diet of nectar supplemented with small arthropods. This low annual fecundity is compensated by extended parental care and a prolonged period of offspring dependency. The maximum recorded lifespan for this species under field conditions, measured at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], is approximately 8.8 years [am = approximately 8.8 years], a longevity figure that situates the Grey sunbird among the longer-lived Nectariniidae and suggests a slow life-history pace consistent with its modest reproductive rate and stable tropical environment.

Developmental milestones in the Grey sunbird are tightly linked to the thermal conditions experienced during the nestling and fledgling periods. When active body temperatures are maintained at approximately 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], young birds achieve fledging at 13 days after hatching [tx = 13 days after hatching], a figure inferred from comparative data on the Golden-winged Sunbird Drepanorhynchus reichenowi. This rapid transition to a flight-capable state may be an adaptation to reduce nest vulnerability to predation and to allow young to follow adults to food sources at an early age. The onset of sexual maturation, by contrast, is considerably delayed relative to fledging. Puberty, defined as the attainment of full gonadal function, is reached at 39 days since birth [tp = 39 days since birth] when individuals are maintained at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This rapid pubertal timeline, while brief in absolute terms, represents a substantial interval post-fledging during which juveniles must refine their foraging skills and accumulate sufficient body reserves to support the energetic demands of reproduction. The disparity between fledging age and puberty age underscores a distinct period of juvenile development dedicated to somatic growth and behavioural maturation.

Adult body mass in Cyanomitra veroxii exhibits a pronounced sexual dimorphism, a trait commonly observed among sunbirds where males tend to be heavier. The ultimate wet weight for females reaches an asymptote of 9.7 grams [Wwi = 9.7 grams], whereas males attain a substantially larger ultimate wet weight of 10.4 grams [Wwi = 10.4 grams]. This approximately 7% mass difference likely confers advantages in male–male competition over territories and floral resources, while the smaller female body size may facilitate more efficient thermoregulation during incubation and reduce overall energetic expenditure during the breeding season. The growth trajectory from the neonatal mass of 1.44 grams [Ww0 = 1.44 grams] to these adult asymptotic masses involves a nearly sevenfold increase in wet weight, a pattern sustained by the high-quality diet of nectar and proteinaceous arthropods provided by the parents. These mass values are consistent with measurements reported for other medium-sized Nectariniidae and highlight the morphological constraints within which the species' life-history schedule operates. The timing of first reproduction is a critical life-history event that determines the generation time of the population.

Under the standard thermal conditions of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], the time since birth at first brood is estimated at 401.5 days [tR = 401.5 days], corresponding to roughly 1.1 years of age. This delay between sexual maturation at 39 days and first reproduction at approximately 401 days indicates a prolonged prereproductive phase during which young birds must establish territories, develop foraging proficiency, and accumulate sufficient energy reserves to sustain the costs of breeding. The interval between reaching puberty and initiating a first clutch likely reflects the challenges of securing a high-quality territory in a competitive environment, as well as the need to attain a body condition that supports successful incubation and chick provisioning. This deferred first breeding, combined with a single annual clutch and a maximum lifespan of 8.8 years [am = 8.8 years], results in a relatively low lifetime reproductive output characteristic of a slow life-history strategy at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. Comparative data from other Nectariniidae suggest that such patterns are common among tropical species, where stable environmental conditions favour investment in adult survival over high fecundity.
